question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$.

Angle $AOB = 80^\circ$.

Work out the size of angle $ACB$, marked $x$. Give a reason for your answer.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="112.5,225.4 180,145 247.5,225.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polyline points="112.5,225.4 180,40 247.5,225.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="112.5" cy="225.4" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="247.5" cy="225.4" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="180" cy="40" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="103.5" y="241.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="256.5" y="241.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="180" y="31" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M167.1 160.3 A20 20 0 0 0 192.9 160.3" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M171.8 62.6 A24 24 0 0 0 188.2 62.6" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="190" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">80°</text><text x="180" y="87" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text><text x="180" y="134" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text></svg>
hint: Both angles stand on the same arc $AB$. Which one is at the centre, and which is at the circumference?
answer: $x = 40^\circ$ (the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference).
solution:
$\angle AOB$ is at the centre and $\angle ACB$ is at the circumference, and both stand on the minor arc $AB$.

The angle at the centre is **twice** the angle at the circumference, so the angle at the circumference is half of it:
$$x = 80^\circ \div 2 = 40^\circ$$

Check: the angle at the centre should be the bigger of the two, and $80^\circ > 40^\circ$.

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$.

Angle $ACB = 35^\circ$.

Work out the size of angle $AOB$, marked $y$. Give a reason for your answer.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="119.8,231 180,145 240.2,231" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polyline points="119.8,231 180,40 240.2,231" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="119.8" cy="231" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="240.2" cy="231" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="180" cy="40" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="111.7" y="247.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="248.3" y="247.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="180" y="31" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M168.5 161.4 A20 20 0 0 0 191.5 161.4" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M172.8 62.9 A24 24 0 0 0 187.2 62.9" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="190" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">y</text><text x="180" y="87" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">35°</text><text x="180" y="134" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text></svg>
hint: This time you know the angle at the circumference. Is the angle at the centre bigger or smaller?
answer: $y = 70^\circ$ (the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference).
solution:
**What changed:** the unknown has moved from the circumference to the centre.

$\angle AOB$ (centre) and $\angle ACB$ (circumference) both stand on arc $AB$, so the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference:
$$y = 2 \times 35^\circ = 70^\circ$$

This time we **double**, because the unknown is the angle at the centre, which is always the larger one.

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. This time $C$ is on the **minor** arc $AB$.

Angle $AOB = 130^\circ$.

Work out the size of angle $ACB$, marked $x$. Give a reason for your answer.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="84.8,100.6 180,145 275.2,100.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polyline points="84.8,100.6 180,250 275.2,100.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="84.8" cy="100.6" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="275.2" cy="100.6" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="180" cy="250" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="72.1" y="99.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="287.9" y="99.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="180" y="269" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M161.9 136.5 A20 20 0 0 1 198.1 136.5" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M167.1 229.8 A24 24 0 0 1 192.9 229.8" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="110" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">130°</text><text x="180" y="213" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text><text x="180" y="166" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text></svg>
hint: Angle $ACB$ stands on the arc $AB$ that does **not** contain $C$. Which angle at the centre stands on that same arc?
solution:
**What changed:** $C$ has moved onto the minor arc, so $\angle ACB$ now stands on the **major** arc $AB$.

The angle at the centre on the major arc is the reflex angle $AOB$:
$$\text{reflex } \angle AOB = 360^\circ - 130^\circ = 230^\circ \quad \text{(angles around a point)}$$

The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference:
$$x = 230^\circ \div 2 = 115^\circ$$

Check: $x$ is obtuse, which matches the diagram. (Halving $130^\circ$ to get $65^\circ$ would use the wrong arc.)

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$.

Angle $AOB = (4x + 10)^\circ$ and angle $ACB = (x + 25)^\circ$.

Work out the value of $x$ and the size of angle $AOB$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="105.8,219.2 180,145 254.2,219.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polyline points="105.8,219.2 180,40 254.2,219.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="105.8" cy="219.2" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="254.2" cy="219.2" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="180" cy="40" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="95.9" y="234.1" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="264.1" y="234.1" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="180" y="31" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M165.9 159.1 A20 20 0 0 0 194.1 159.1" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M170.8 62.2 A24 24 0 0 0 189.2 62.2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="190" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(4x + 10)°</text><text x="180" y="120" fill="currentColor" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(x + 25)°</text><text x="195" y="148" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text></svg>
hint: Write an equation using "angle at the centre $= 2 \times$ angle at the circumference".
solution:
**What changed:** the angles are now algebraic expressions, but the theorem is the same.

Angle at the centre $= 2 \times$ angle at the circumference (both on arc $AB$):
$$4x + 10 = 2(x + 25)$$
$$4x + 10 = 2x + 50$$
$$2x = 40 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 20$$

So $\angle AOB = 4(20) + 10 = 90^\circ$ and $\angle ACB = 20 + 25 = 45^\circ$.

Check: $90^\circ = 2 \times 45^\circ$.

question:
$A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are points on a circle, so $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Angle $DAB = 74^\circ$ and angle $ABC = 103^\circ$.

Work out the sizes of angle $BCD$ (marked $x$) and angle $CDA$ (marked $y$). Give reasons.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="81.3,180.9 208.9,245.9 284.4,156 208.9,44.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="81.3" cy="180.9" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="68.2" y="190.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><path d="M95 166.3 A20 20 0 0 1 99.2 190" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="120.7" y="179" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">74°</text><circle cx="208.9" cy="245.9" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="212.8" y="264.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><path d="M191.1 236.9 A20 20 0 0 1 221.8 230.6" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="201" y="211.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">103°</text><circle cx="284.4" cy="156" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="298.3" y="162.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M271.6 171.3 A20 20 0 0 1 273.2 139.4" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="244.5" y="158.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text><circle cx="208.9" cy="44.1" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="212.8" y="35.6" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><path d="M220.1 60.6 A20 20 0 0 1 195.3 58.7" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="205.8" y="88.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">y</text></svg>
hint: Which angle is **opposite** angle $A$? Which is opposite angle $B$?
answer: $x = 106^\circ$, $y = 77^\circ$ (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$)
solution:
All four vertices lie on the circle, so $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral and **opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$**.

$\angle BCD$ is opposite $\angle DAB$:
$$x = 180^\circ - 74^\circ = 106^\circ$$

$\angle CDA$ is opposite $\angle ABC$:
$$y = 180^\circ - 103^\circ = 77^\circ$$

Check: $74^\circ + 103^\circ + 106^\circ + 77^\circ = 360^\circ$, as for any quadrilateral.

question:
$PA$ and $PB$ are tangents to a circle with centre $O$, touching the circle at $A$ and $B$.

Angle $APB = 64^\circ$.

(a) Work out the size of angle $AOB$.

(b) Work out the size of angle $OAB$.

Give a reason for each step.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="125" cy="145" r="80" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="276" y1="145" x2="140.3" y2="60.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="276" y1="145" x2="140.3" y2="229.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="125" y1="145" x2="167.4" y2="77.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="125" y1="145" x2="167.4" y2="212.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="167.4" y1="77.2" x2="167.4" y2="212.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="125" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="167.4" cy="77.2" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="167.4" cy="212.8" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="276" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="111" y="150" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text x="174.8" y="70.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="174.8" y="229.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="289" y="150" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">P</text><path d="M253.9 131.2 A26 26 0 0 0 253.9 158.8" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="226" y="150" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">64°</text></svg>
hint: A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at $90^\circ$. Then look at quadrilateral $OAPB$.
solution:
**(a)** $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$ (a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact).

Angles in quadrilateral $OAPB$ add up to $360^\circ$:
$$\angle AOB = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$$

**(b)** $OA = OB$ (radii), so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal:
$$\angle OAB = \frac{180^\circ - 116^\circ}{2} = 32^\circ$$

Alternative for (b): $PA = PB$ (tangents from an external point are equal), so $\angle PAB = \frac{180^\circ - 64^\circ}{2} = 58^\circ$ and $\angle OAB = 90^\circ - 58^\circ = 32^\circ$.

question:
The chords $AB$ and $CD$ of a circle intersect at $E$.

$AE = 6$ cm, $EB = 4$ cm and $CE = 3$ cm.

(a) Work out the length $ED$, marked $x$.

In a different circle, two chords $PQ$ and $RS$ intersect at $F$. $PF = 5$ cm, $FQ = 8$ cm and $RF = 4$ cm.

(b) Work out the length of the chord $RS$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="108" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="244.7" y1="58.5" x2="234.5" y2="238.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="288" y1="144.5" x2="106.8" y2="224.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="244.7" cy="58.5" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="234.5" cy="238.2" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="288" cy="144.5" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="106.8" cy="224.5" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="238.6" cy="166.3" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="253" y="52.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="241.6" y="255.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="302" y="149.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="97.4" y="239.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="252.5" y="176.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">E</text><text x="228.6" y="116.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">6</text><text x="223.6" y="206.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">4</text><text x="268.5" y="172.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">3</text><text x="178" y="212.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text></svg>
hint: For two chords crossing inside a circle, the products of the two pieces of each chord are equal: $AE \times EB = CE \times ED$.
solution:
**Intersecting chords theorem:** when two chords cross, the products of their segments are equal.

**(a)**
$$AE \times EB = CE \times ED$$
$$6 \times 4 = 3x$$
$$24 = 3x \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 8 \text{ cm}$$

**(b)**
$$PF \times FQ = RF \times FS$$
$$5 \times 8 = 4 \times FS \quad\Rightarrow\quad FS = 10 \text{ cm}$$

The question asks for the **whole chord**:
$$RS = RF + FS = 4 + 10 = 14 \text{ cm}$$

The minor arc $AC$ measures $40^\circ$ and the arc $BD$ (on the far side from $P$) measures $130^\circ$.

(a) Work out the size of angle $APC$.

(b) Work out the size of angle $BXD$.

(US Geometry: the measure of an arc equals the angle it subtends at the centre.)

hint: An angle formed by two secants **outside** the circle is half the **difference** of the intercepted arcs. An angle formed by two chords **inside** the circle is half the **sum** of the intercepted arcs.
solution:
**(a)** $P$ is outside the circle, so the angle between the two secants is half the difference of the intercepted arcs (far arc minus near arc):
$$\angle APC = \tfrac{1}{2}(130^\circ - 40^\circ) = 45^\circ$$

**(b)** $X$ is inside the circle. Angle $BXD$ and its vertical angle $AXC$ intercept arcs $BD$ and $AC$, so
$$\angle BXD = \tfrac{1}{2}(130^\circ + 40^\circ) = 85^\circ$$

**Why these work (using inscribed angles):** an inscribed angle is half its arc, so $\angle ADC = 20^\circ$ and $\angle BAD = 65^\circ$.

* In triangle $APD$, the exterior angle $\angle BAD = \angle APD + \angle ADP$, so $\angle APC = 65^\circ - 20^\circ = 45^\circ$.
* $X$ lies on $BC$, so $\angle BXD$ is the exterior angle of triangle $CXD$ at $X$: $\angle BXD = \angle XDC + \angle XCD = \angle ADC + \angle BCD = 20^\circ + 65^\circ = 85^\circ$ (since $\angle BCD = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 130^\circ$).

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. Angle $AOB = 124^\circ$. Priya is asked to find angle $ACB$, marked $x$.

Priya's working is shown below.

> $OACB$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, so opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$.
>
> $x = 180^\circ - 124^\circ = 56^\circ$

(a) Identify Priya's mistake and explain why her reasoning is wrong.

(b) Work out the correct value of $x$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="180,145 87.3,194.3 161.8,41.6 272.7,194.3" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="87.3" cy="194.3" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="272.7" cy="194.3" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="161.8" cy="41.6" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="74.9" y="205.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="285.1" y="205.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="159.3" y="32.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="180" y="134" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text><path d="M162.3 154.4 A20 20 0 0 0 197.7 154.4" stroke="#3b82f6" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="184" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">124°</text><path d="M151.2 63.2 A24 24 0 0 0 175.9 61" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="165.4" y="88.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text></svg>
hint: Is every vertex of $OACB$ on the circle?
answer: (a) $OACB$ is not a cyclic quadrilateral because $O$ is the centre, not a point on the circle. (b) $x = 62^\circ$
solution:
**(a)** The error is in the first line. A cyclic quadrilateral must have **all four vertices on the circumference**. $O$ is the centre of the circle, so $OACB$ is not cyclic and the "opposite angles add to $180^\circ$" rule does not apply.

**(b)** $\angle AOB$ is at the centre and $\angle ACB$ is at the circumference, both standing on the minor arc $AB$. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference:
$$x = 124^\circ \div 2 = 62^\circ$$

Note how close Priya's answer looks ($56^\circ$ against $62^\circ$): a wrong theorem can still give a believable number, so always check the conditions of a theorem before using it.

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle. $SAT$ is the tangent to the circle at $A$.

Angle $SAB = 50^\circ$ and angle $TAC = 64^\circ$.

Tom is asked to find angle $ABC$, marked $y$. His working is shown below.

> By the alternate segment theorem, the angle between the tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
>
> So $y = \angle SAB = 50^\circ$.

(a) Explain the mistake Tom has made.

(b) Work out the correct size of angle $ABC$, and also the size of angle $ACB$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="130" r="100" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="40" y1="230" x2="320" y2="230" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="180,230 81.5,112.6 258.8,68.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="230" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="81.5" cy="112.6" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="258.8" cy="68.4" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="180" y="251" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="67.7" y="115.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="269.8" y="64.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="44" y="223" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">S</text><text x="316" y="223" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">T</text><path d="M158.1 204 A34 34 0 0 0 146 230" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="132.9" y="213" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">50°</text><path d="M194.9 199.4 A34 34 0 0 1 214 230" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="224.1" y="207.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">64°</text><path d="M95.7 129.5 A22 22 0 0 0 102.9 107.3" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="117.7" y="129.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">y</text></svg>
hint: Angle $SAB$ is made with chord $AB$. Angle $ABC$ is at $B$, so it is **not** the angle subtended by chord $AB$. Which chord does angle $ABC$ stand on?
answer: (a) He paired the tangent–chord angle at chord $AB$ with an angle at an end of that same chord, instead of the angle subtended by the chord in the alternate segment. (b) $\angle ABC = 64^\circ$, $\angle ACB = 50^\circ$
solution:
**(a)** The alternate segment theorem says: the angle between the tangent and the chord $AB$ equals the angle that **chord $AB$ subtends** at a point on the circle in the alternate segment, i.e. at $C$. So $\angle SAB$ equals $\angle ACB$, not $\angle ABC$. Angle $ABC$ has its vertex at $B$, an end of chord $AB$, so it is in the wrong place to be matched with $\angle SAB$.

**(b)** Angle $ABC$ stands on chord $AC$. The tangent makes angle $TAC = 64^\circ$ with chord $AC$, and $B$ is in the alternate segment, so
$$\angle ABC = \angle TAC = 64^\circ \quad \text{(alternate segment theorem)}$$

Similarly, angle $ACB$ stands on chord $AB$:
$$\angle ACB = \angle SAB = 50^\circ \quad \text{(alternate segment theorem)}$$

Check: angles on the straight line $SAT$ give $\angle BAC = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 64^\circ = 66^\circ$, and $64^\circ + 50^\circ + 66^\circ = 180^\circ$ in triangle $ABC$.

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. Angle $AOB = 140^\circ$.

Sam says:

> "Angle $ACB$ is $90^\circ$, because it is the angle in a semicircle."

Is Sam correct? Explain your answer, and find the actual size of angle $ACB$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="81.3,180.9 170.8,40.4 278.7,180.9" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="180" y1="145" x2="81.3" y2="180.9" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="180" y1="145" x2="278.7" y2="180.9" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="81.3" cy="180.9" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="278.7" cy="180.9" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="170.8" cy="40.4" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="68.2" y="190.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="291.8" y="190.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="169.6" y="31.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="180" y="134" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text><path d="M166.8 149.8 A14 14 0 0 0 193.2 149.8" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="174" fill="currentColor" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">140°</text><path d="M158 60.6 A24 24 0 0 0 185.5 59.4" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="172.7" y="87.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">x</text></svg>
hint: What must be true about chord $AB$ for the "angle in a semicircle" theorem to apply? Is it true here?
answer: No. $AB$ is not a diameter (angle $AOB$ is $140^\circ$, not $180^\circ$), so the theorem does not apply. Angle $ACB = 70^\circ$.
solution:
The angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$ only when the chord $AB$ is a **diameter**, i.e. passes through the centre $O$. Then $A$, $O$ and $B$ would be in a straight line and $\angle AOB$ would be $180^\circ$.

Here $\angle AOB = 140^\circ \ne 180^\circ$, so $AB$ does not pass through $O$: it is not a diameter, and $C$ is not on a semicircle. Sam is **not correct**.

Instead use "the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference" (both on minor arc $AB$):
$$\angle ACB = 140^\circ \div 2 = 70^\circ$$

(Seen another way: the semicircle theorem is just the special case $\angle AOB = 180^\circ$, giving $180^\circ \div 2 = 90^\circ$.)

question:
A drainage pipe has a circular cross-section. Water lies in the bottom of the pipe.

The surface of the water is a horizontal chord of width 48 cm. The water is 8 cm deep at its deepest point.

Work out the internal diameter of the pipe.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><path d="M111 227 A115 115 0 0 0 249 227 Z" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="none"/><circle cx="180" cy="135" r="115" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="111" y1="227" x2="249" y2="227" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="180" y1="20" x2="180" y2="250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="180" cy="135" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="194" y="140" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text><polyline points="188,227 188,219 180,219" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="111" y1="227" x2="111" y2="266" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><line x1="249" y1="227" x2="249" y2="266" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><line x1="111" y1="262" x2="249" y2="262" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2"/><polygon points="111,262 118,258.5 118,265.5" fill="currentColor"/><polygon points="249,262 242,265.5 242,258.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="180" y="283" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">48 cm</text><text x="189" y="242.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="12" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">8 cm</text></svg>
hint: Extend the vertical depth line into a full diameter. It cuts the water-surface chord into two halves of 24 cm. Now use the intersecting chords theorem (or Pythagoras).
solution:
The vertical line through the deepest point passes through the centre (the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord), so it is a diameter, and it cuts the 48 cm chord into two pieces of 24 cm.

Let the diameter be $d$ cm. The diameter is split by the chord into 8 cm (below) and $(d - 8)$ cm (above).

**Intersecting chords theorem:**
$$24 \times 24 = 8 \times (d - 8)$$
$$576 = 8(d - 8)$$
$$d - 8 = 72 \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = 80$$

The internal diameter is **80 cm**.

Check with Pythagoras: radius $40$, centre is $40 - 8 = 32$ cm above the water, and $32^2 + 24^2 = 1024 + 576 = 1600 = 40^2$.

question:
A lighthouse lamp $L$ is 52 m above sea level. Model the Earth as a sphere with centre $O$ and radius 6370 km. The line of sight from $L$ to the horizon touches the Earth's surface at $H$, so $LH$ is a tangent. The line from $L$ through the base $B$ of the lighthouse passes through $O$ and meets the Earth again at $F$.

The diagram is not drawn to scale.

(a) Use the tangent–secant theorem to show that the distance $LH$, in km, is given by $LH^2 = h(h + 12\,740)$, where $h$ is the height of the lamp in km.

(b) Work out the distance from the lamp to the horizon. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

(c) A coastguard says the lamp must be visible from a boat 40 km away (ignore the height of the boat). How high above sea level would the lamp need to be? Give your answer to the nearest metre.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="120" cy="175" r="95" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120" y1="80" x2="120" y2="25" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4"/><line x1="120" y1="25" x2="230.3" y2="159.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120" y1="80" x2="120" y2="270" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="120" y1="175" x2="193.5" y2="114.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="187.8,107.9 180.9,113.6 186.6,120.5" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="120" cy="25" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="193.5" cy="114.8" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="120" cy="80" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="120" cy="175" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="120" cy="270" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="106" y="30" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">L</text><text x="205.1" y="110.3" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">H</text><text x="106" y="180" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text x="106" y="97" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="106" y="283" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">F</text><text x="102" y="57.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">h</text><text x="174.8" y="161.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">6370 km</text></svg>
hint: From the external point $L$, the tangent squared equals (distance to the near intersection) $\times$ (distance to the far intersection) along the line through $O$.
solution:
**(a)** The line from $L$ through $O$ is a secant: it meets the sphere at $B$ (distance $h$ from $L$) and again at $F$, the far end of the diameter $BF$ (distance $h + 2 \times 6370 = h + 12\,740$ from $L$).

Tangent–secant theorem (the tangent squared equals the product of the secant segments):
$$LH^2 = h(h + 12\,740)$$

(Equivalently, by Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle $OHL$, since the tangent is perpendicular to the radius: $LH^2 = (6370 + h)^2 - 6370^2 = h^2 + 12\,740h$.)

**(b)** $h = 52$ m $= 0.052$ km:
$$LH^2 = 0.052 \times 12\,740.052 = 662.4827$$
$$LH = 25.7387\ldots \approx 25.7 \text{ km}$$

**(c)** We need $LH = 40$:
$$h(h + 12\,740) = 1600 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h^2 + 12\,740h - 1600 = 0$$

Using the quadratic formula (positive root):
$$h = \frac{-12\,740 + \sqrt{12\,740^2 + 4 \times 1600}}{2} = 0.12559\ldots \text{ km}$$

So the lamp would need to be about **126 m** above sea level. (Since $h$ is tiny compared with 12 740, $h \approx 1600 \div 12\,740 \approx 0.1256$ km gives the same answer.)

question:
$A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. $TA$ is the tangent to the circle at $A$.

Angle $TAB = 68^\circ$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="175" cy="140" r="100" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="18.6" y1="189.5" x2="244.2" y2="271.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="140.8,234 273.5,157.4 264.9,96.2 88.4,90" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="140.8" y1="234" x2="264.9" y2="96.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="175" y1="140" x2="140.8" y2="234" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="175" y1="140" x2="264.9" y2="96.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="175" cy="140" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="140.8" cy="234" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="264.9" cy="96.2" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="88.4" cy="90" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="273.5" cy="157.4" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="135.3" y="254" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="277.5" y="95" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="76.3" y="88" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="287.3" y="164.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="171" y="131" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text x="255.4" y="280.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">T</text><path d="M160.9 211.7 A30 30 0 0 1 169 244.2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="186.6" y="235" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">68°</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write down the size of angle $ACB$. Give a reason for your answer.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Work out the size of angle $OAB$. Give a reason for your answer.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Work out the size of angle $ADB$. You must show your working and give reasons.

hint: (a) The tangent and chord $AB$ make $68^\circ$; which angle is in the alternate segment? (b) What angle does a tangent make with a radius? (c) $ADBC$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.
solution:
**(a)** $\angle ACB = 68^\circ$ (B1)

The angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment. (B1)

**(b)** $\angle OAT = 90^\circ$ because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. (B1 for the reason)
$$\angle OAB = 90^\circ - 68^\circ = 22^\circ \quad \text{(B1)}$$

**(c)** $A$, $D$, $B$, $C$ all lie on the circle, so $ADBC$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, and $\angle ADB$ is opposite $\angle ACB$. (M1)

Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$:
$$\angle ADB = 180^\circ - 68^\circ = 112^\circ \quad \text{(A1)}$$

Alternative for (c): $\angle AOB = 2 \times 68^\circ = 136^\circ$ (angle at centre), so reflex $\angle AOB = 224^\circ$ and $\angle ADB = 224^\circ \div 2 = 112^\circ$. (M1 A1)

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle. The tangent to the circle at $A$ meets the line $CB$ extended at $T$.

$TA = 12$ cm and $TB = 8$ cm.

(a) Work out the length of $BC$.

(b) Given also that $AB = 9$ cm, work out the length of $AC$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="187.5" cy="138.3" r="84.4" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="25" y1="195" x2="250" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="25" y1="195" x2="124.2" y2="82.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="124.2" y1="82.5" x2="125" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="124.2" y1="82.5" x2="250" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="124.2" cy="82.5" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="125" cy="195" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="250" cy="195" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="25" cy="195" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="124.2" y="73.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="127" y="218" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="262" y="212" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="17" y="216" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">T</text><text x="75" y="216" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">8 cm</text><text x="54.6" y="137.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">12 cm</text></svg>
hint: For (a) use the tangent–secant theorem from $T$. For (b), the alternate segment theorem gives $\angle TAB = \angle ACB$; look for two similar triangles that share the angle at $T$.
solution:
**(a)** From the external point $T$, $TA$ is a tangent and $TBC$ is a secant, so
$$TA^2 = TB \times TC \quad\Rightarrow\quad 144 = 8 \times TC \quad\Rightarrow\quad TC = 18 \text{ cm}$$
$$BC = TC - TB = 18 - 8 = 10 \text{ cm}$$

**(b)** Compare triangles $TAB$ and $TCA$:

* $\angle ATB = \angle CTA$ (the same angle at $T$);
* $\angle TAB = \angle TCA$ (alternate segment theorem: the angle between tangent $TA$ and chord $AB$ equals the angle $ACB$ in the alternate segment).

So the triangles are similar (AA), with $T \leftrightarrow T$, $A \leftrightarrow C$, $B \leftrightarrow A$. Corresponding sides are in the same ratio:
$$\frac{AB}{CA} = \frac{TA}{TC} = \frac{TB}{TA} = \frac{12}{18} = \frac{2}{3}$$

(Check: $\frac{TB}{TA} = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$ too, which is exactly the tangent–secant theorem again.)

$$\frac{9}{AC} = \frac{2}{3} \quad\Rightarrow\quad AC = \frac{27}{2} = 13.5 \text{ cm}$$

question:
$ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. The diagram is not drawn to scale.

Angle $DAB = (3x + y)^\circ$, angle $ABC = (2x + 3y)^\circ$, angle $BCD = (x + 2y)^\circ$ and angle $CDA = (4x - y)^\circ$.

(a) Work out the values of $x$ and $y$.

(b) Hence show that $BD$ is a diameter of the circle.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><circle cx="180" cy="145" r="105" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="81.3,180.9 198.2,248.4 284.6,154.2 161.8,41.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="81.3" cy="180.9" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="68.2" y="190.7" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><path d="M91.3 163.6 A20 20 0 0 1 98.7 190.9" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="135.4" y="171.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(3x + y)°</text><circle cx="198.2" cy="248.4" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="200.7" y="267.2" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><path d="M180.9 238.4 A20 20 0 0 1 211.7 233.7" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="189.7" y="198.1" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(2x + 3y)°</text><circle cx="284.6" cy="154.2" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="298.5" y="160.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><path d="M271.1 168.9 A20 20 0 0 1 269.9 140.6" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="228.7" y="161.6" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(x + 2y)°</text><circle cx="161.8" cy="41.6" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="159.3" y="32.8" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><path d="M176.5 55.1 A20 20 0 0 1 151.8 58.9" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="170.3" y="101.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="13" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">(4x − y)°</text></svg>
hint: Write two equations, one for each pair of opposite angles, then solve them simultaneously.
answer: (a) $x = 18$, $y = 36$ (b) $\angle DAB = 90^\circ$, so $BD$ subtends a right angle at the circumference and is a diameter.
solution:
**(a)** Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to $180^\circ$.

$\angle A + \angle C$:
$$(3x + y) + (x + 2y) = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 4x + 3y = 180 \quad (1)$$

$\angle B + \angle D$:
$$(2x + 3y) + (4x - y) = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 6x + 2y = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3x + y = 90 \quad (2)$$

From (2), $y = 90 - 3x$. Substitute into (1):
$$4x + 3(90 - 3x) = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 4x + 270 - 9x = 180 \quad\Rightarrow\quad -5x = -90 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 18$$
$$y = 90 - 54 = 36$$

Angles: $\angle A = 90^\circ$, $\angle B = 144^\circ$, $\angle C = 90^\circ$, $\angle D = 36^\circ$ (total $360^\circ$ ✓).

**(b)** $\angle DAB = 3(18) + 36 = 90^\circ$. This is the angle subtended by chord $BD$ at $A$ on the circumference. The angle at the centre on the same arc is $2 \times 90^\circ = 180^\circ$, so $B$, $O$ and $D$ lie on a straight line: $BD$ passes through the centre and is a diameter. (This is the converse of the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem.)

question:
Triangle $ABC$ is drawn inside a circle with centre $O$ and radius $R$, with all three vertices on the circle. Angle $BAC$ is acute. $BD$ is a diameter of the circle.

(a) Prove that $BC = 2R \sin A$, where $A$ is the size of angle $BAC$.

(b) In a triangle $ABC$, angle $BAC = 40^\circ$ and $BC = 9$ cm. Work out the radius of the circle that passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

hint: Use two circle theorems: one gives you a right angle in triangle $BCD$, the other tells you that angle $BDC$ equals angle $BAC$. Then use right-angled trigonometry.
solution:
**(a)** Join $D$ to $C$.

* $\angle BCD = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle, since $BD$ is a diameter).
* $\angle BDC = \angle BAC = A$ (angles in the same segment, both standing on chord $BC$; $A$ and $D$ are on the same side of $BC$ because $A$ is acute).

In right-angled triangle $BCD$, $BC$ is opposite the angle at $D$ and the hypotenuse is the diameter $BD = 2R$:
$$\sin A = \sin \angle BDC = \frac{BC}{BD} = \frac{BC}{2R}$$

Therefore $BC = 2R \sin A$. $\blacksquare$

(This is why the sine rule $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$ works: every ratio equals the diameter $2R$ of the circumcircle.)

**(b)**
$$9 = 2R \sin 40^\circ \quad\Rightarrow\quad R = \frac{9}{2 \sin 40^\circ} = 7.00076\ldots$$

$R \approx 7$ cm.

question:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. $SAT$ is the tangent at $A$, and $C$ lies on the major arc $AB$. Angle $TAB = \theta$, where $\theta$ is acute.

Prove that angle $ACB = \theta$ (the alternate segment theorem).

You may use any of the other circle theorems, but you must give a reason for every step.

hint: Join $O$ to $A$ and to $B$. Find angle $OAB$ using the tangent, then use the isosceles triangle $OAB$ to find angle $AOB$ in terms of $\theta$.
answer: Proof: $\angle OAB = 90^\circ - \theta$, $\angle OBA = 90^\circ - \theta$, so $\angle AOB = 2\theta$ and $\angle ACB = \theta$.
solution:
Join $OA$ and $OB$.

1. $\angle OAT = 90^\circ$ (a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact), so
$$\angle OAB = 90^\circ - \theta$$

2. $OA = OB$ (radii), so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles and
$$\angle OBA = \angle OAB = 90^\circ - \theta \quad \text{(base angles of an isosceles triangle)}$$

3. Angles in triangle $OAB$ add up to $180^\circ$:
$$\angle AOB = 180^\circ - 2(90^\circ - \theta) = 2\theta$$

4. $\angle AOB$ (at the centre) and $\angle ACB$ (at the circumference, $C$ on the major arc) stand on the same minor arc $AB$, so
$$\angle ACB = \tfrac{1}{2}\angle AOB = \theta \quad \text{(angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference)}$$

Hence the angle between the tangent and the chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. $\blacksquare$

Note: $C$ is on the opposite side of chord $AB$ from the angle $\theta$ — that is what "alternate" means.
